query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Ti to equal‐atomic NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic NbMoTaW exhibiting a single-phase BCC structure, excellent yield strength at 1600 °C, and predicted irradiation resistance, but with very poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low atomic percentage (e.g., 5–10 at%) of titanium into NbMoTaW during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Evaluations performed at room temperature (to assess ductility), at 1600 °C (to measure high-temperature mechanical strength), and under controlled irradiation conditions (e.g., He ion irradiation) to monitor defect evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Substitutional Ti atoms are expected to modify local grain-boundary chemistry and cohesion while preserving the overall single-phase BCC structure. This improved boundary cohesion eases dislocation activity at low temperatures without promoting secondary phase formation.
generation.mechanism: The Ti addition reduces intergranular embrittlement by enhancing grain-boundary cohesion and altering dislocation nucleation barriers, thereby permitting increased plastic strain at room temperature. At the same time, the low concentration is kept below a threshold to prevent any deleterious microstructural changes that could impair the high-temperature strength or the inherent irradiation defect recombination benefits of the NbMoTaW matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-alloyed variant is expected to exhibit a significant increase in room-temperature ductility (higher plastic strain during compressive/tensile testing) while retaining similar yield strengths at 1600 °C and maintaining its resistance to irradiation-induced defect clustering.
generation.baseline: Pure equal-atomic NbMoTaW BCC alloy with high yield strength at high temperature and calculated irradiation resistance but low room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only for a narrow Ti doping range (approximately 5–10 at%). Exceeding this range may lead to secondary phase precipitation or altered lattice parameters that could compromise high-temperature performance or irradiation stability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative enhancement in room-temperature ductility and the precise limit for Ti concentration without affecting high-temperature properties are uncertain. Microstructural evolution under prolonged irradiation with Ti remains to be fully verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with varied Ti content (e.g., 0, 5, and 10 at%). Characterize the microstructure using TEM to ensure retention of the BCC phase and measure grain boundary features. Conduct mechanical testing at room temperature to quantify ductility improvements, perform high-temperature mechanical tests at 1600 °C, and subject samples to controlled He ion irradiation. Compare defect densities and mechanical property changes with the undoped baseline.
measurements: Irradiation-induced defect density via TEM after irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., <10% increase in plastic strain) or if high-temperature yield strength or irradiation resistance degrades (e.g., >10% drop in yield strength or increased defect accumulation compared to pure NbMoTaW), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
